paper_a.title: Stochastic Relaxation, Gibbs Distributions, and the Bayesian Restoration of Images

paper_b.title: Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines

metadata.description: Geman & Geman's Gibbs Sampler is the specialization of the Metropolis algorithm to proposals drawn from the local conditional (full-conditional) distribution, which yields acceptance probability one. Both papers construct an MCMC sampler with the same Boltzmann/Gibbs target and prove convergence/ergodicity by similar Markov-chain arguments. Geman-Geman additionally introduces the simulated-annealing schedule for MAP estimation; Metropolis instead uses the chain at fixed temperature to compute equilibrium averages.

matches.explanation: Gibbs Sampler (paper A) and Metropolis algorithm (paper B) are both site/particle-by-site MCMC samplers targeting a Boltzmann distribution $\propto e^{-E/T}$. They play the same role: both are iterative local-update MCMC samplers with the canonical/Gibbs distribution as equilibrium. Mathematically the Gibbs Sampler is the special case of Metropolis-Hastings with proposal equal to the full conditional, in which $\Delta E$-based rejection becomes always-accept. Paper A (DP384.5/AP384.1) updates by drawing $X_s$ from the local characteristic; Paper B (AP385.1) proposes uniform displacements and accepts via $\min(1,e^{-\Delta E/kT})$. Same equilibrium target, different proposal/acceptance mechanism — analogous, not exact.

Paper A explicitly cites the Metropolis algorithm (AP384.2, origin: external, citation Metropolis-Rosenbluth-Teller 1953) which is exactly the algorithm contributed in paper B (AP385.1). The cited statement ($\min(1,e^{-\beta\Delta\mathcal{E}})$ acceptance) matches paper B's algorithm verbatim. This is an external↔paper-origin alignment that confirms paper A consciously builds on paper B.

Both define the target equilibrium distribution as a Boltzmann/Gibbs distribution. Paper A's Gibbs distribution $\pi(\omega)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(\omega)/T}$ (DP384.3) and paper B's canonical-ensemble average with weight $e^{-E/kT}$ (DP385.3) are the same object: Boltzmann weights normalized by a partition function. Paper A's $U$ decomposes over cliques while paper B's $E$ decomposes over pair potentials, but both are sums of local interactions.

Local characteristic vs trial move: both define the per-coordinate transition kernel of the chain. Paper A's local characteristic (DP384.5) is the conditional $\pi(x_s\mid x_{r\neq s})$ from which the Gibbs Sampler proposes (and always accepts). Paper B's trial move (DP385.4) is a uniform-in-square symmetric proposal that is then filtered by the Metropolis acceptance test. Same role (local proposal kernel) but different mechanisms — the Gibbs choice eliminates rejection, while Metropolis decouples proposal from target.

Paper A's potential $\{V_C\}$ over cliques (DP384.4) and paper B's pairwise potential $E=\tfrac12\sum_{i\neq j} V(d_{ij})$ (DP385.2) both define a local energy decomposition. Paper B's pair potential is the special case of paper A's clique potentials restricted to 2-cliques (edges). Analogous via specialization: physical pair potential is a graph-theoretic clique potential of order 2.

Paper B states the problem as evaluating the canonical-ensemble average $\langle F\rangle=\int F e^{-E/kT}/\int e^{-E/kT}$ (ProbP385.1), which combines paper A's two problems: sampling from a Gibbs distribution (ProbP384.2) and computing expectations under it (ProbP384.3). Same goal — produce Boltzmann-distributed samples and use them to estimate observables — phrased once in physics language, twice in probability language.

Both are convergence theorems for the proposed MCMC sampler at fixed temperature. Paper A's Theorem A (TP384.3) proves $P(X(t)=\omega\mid X(0)=\eta)\to\pi(\omega)$ for the Gibbs Sampler under an infinite-visits condition. Paper B's TP385.1 proves the Metropolis chain is ergodic with stationary distribution $\nu_r\propto e^{-E_r/kT}$. Same conclusion (convergence to the Boltzmann target) for the two distinct chains; the precise hypotheses (visiting schedule vs symmetric proposal) differ. Paper A's proof is far more rigorous (contraction lemma over sweeps); paper B's is a heuristic flow argument.

Paper A's Theorem C (TP384.5, ergodic theorem: $n^{-1}\sum_t Y(X(t))\to\mathbb{E}_\pi Y$ a.s.) is the law-of-large-numbers companion to paper B's convergence claim and is implicit in paper B's use of $F=(1/M)\sum F_j$ as an estimator. Paper B does not state a separate ergodic theorem but its TP385.1 is what justifies the time-average estimator — analogous role.

Both proofs establish convergence of the Markov chain to the Boltzmann distribution. Paper A (PP384.2) uses an explicit transition matrix, verifies invariance $\pi M_t=\pi$, and proves a contraction inequality over sweeps. Paper B (PP385.1) gives a flow-style argument: net flow between two states vanishes iff the canonical ratio holds, plus an ergodicity claim. Same conceptual structure (invariance + ergodicity) but paper A is mathematically rigorous while paper B is physical/heuristic.

Composite L2 alignment for the convergence-proof step DAGs (parent match emitted above). Paper A's three steps — set up transition matrix and invariance (PSP384.1), prove contraction (PSP384.2), conclude (PSP384.3) — parallel paper B's four steps — symmetric proposal (PSP385.1), ergodicity (PSP385.2), net-flow algebra (PSP385.3), conclude (PSP385.4). Both decompositions follow the same logical skeleton: establish the invariant measure (via either explicit invariance or detailed balance), establish reachability, combine into convergence. Paper B substitutes detailed balance for paper A's contraction lemma.

Composite L2 alignment for the algorithm step decompositions (parent match AP384.1↔AP385.1 emitted above). Step-by-step: initialize (ASP384.1↔ASP385.1), select/sweep over coordinate (ASP384.2↔ASP385.2), local update (ASP384.3↔ASP385.3+ASP385.4: paper A samples from the conditional, paper B proposes+accepts), iterate (ASP384.4↔ASP385.6). Paper B has an extra explicit running-average step (ASP385.5) which paper A leaves implicit to the ergodic theorem. The structural parallel is exact; the difference at the update step is precisely the Gibbs-vs-Metropolis distinction.

Paper A's simulated-annealing concept (AP384.3, cited from Kirkpatrick et al. 1983) has no counterpart in paper B, which uses the Metropolis chain only at fixed temperature for equilibrium calculations. Annealing is a later innovation built on top of Metropolis.

Paper A's annealing convergence theorem (Theorem B, TP384.4: $T(t)\ge N\Delta/\log t$ implies convergence to uniform on the MAP set $\Omega_0$) is paper-original to Geman-Geman. Paper B uses no temperature schedule and proves nothing about MAP recovery — its Metropolis chain is run at a single $T$.

Annealing schedule (DP384.9) and minimal-energy set $\Omega_0$ (DP384.10) are paper-A-specific concepts tied to Theorem B; paper B has no analogue (no cooling schedule, no MAP/ground-state objective).
Paper A's proof of the annealing theorem (PP384.3, Lemmas 2-3 with the divergence-of-series argument) has no counterpart in paper B since paper B has no annealing claim.

Neighborhood system / graph (DP384.1) and Markov Random Field (DP384.2) are graphical-model formalism specific to paper A's image-restoration framing. Paper B works on a fixed 2D simulation cell with periodic boundary conditions and pair potentials — no abstract neighborhood system or MRF formalism is introduced.
Hammersley-Clifford theorem (TP384.1, MRF↔Gibbs equivalence) is cited in paper A and has no analogue in paper B.

Image-restoration-specific definitions: image model with line process (DP384.6), degraded image model (DP384.7), posterior energy $U^P$ (DP384.8). Paper B's domain is statistical mechanics of an N-particle fluid, with no image, degradation, or Bayesian posterior.
Posterior-is-Gibbsian theorem (TP384.2) is the Bayesian image-restoration cornerstone of paper A; paper B has no Bayesian posterior.
Proof of TP384.2 is paper-A-original; no analogue in paper B.

MAP image restoration problem (ProbP384.1) is paper-A-original. Paper B's problem is the equation-of-state / equilibrium-average evaluation, a sampling/expectation problem rather than an optimization problem.

Periodic boundary conditions and minimum-image distance (DP385.1) are paper-B-specific physical-simulation conventions. Paper A uses a finite lattice $Z_m$ without periodicity (boundary handled by neighborhood system).

Paper B's sample-average estimator $F=(1/M)\sum F_j$ (DP385.5) is implicit in paper A through the ergodic theorem TP384.5 but is not given as a separate definition node. Listed as none on the A side for completeness.
Radial distribution count $N_m$ (DP385.6) is a physics observable specific to paper B's analysis of pair correlations; no counterpart in paper A's image-restoration setting.

Cluster integrals $A_{i,k}$ (DP385.7) and the virial expansion (EP385.2, EP385.3) are paper-B-original perturbative analyses comparing the Monte Carlo data to a low-density expansion. No analogue in paper A.
Clausius virial theorem (EP385.1, cited external) is used by paper B to convert configurational averages into pressures. No counterpart in paper A.
2D rigid-sphere equation of state (TP385.2: $PA=NkT(1+\pi d_0^2\bar n/2)$) is paper-B-original physics. No counterpart in paper A.
Paper B's standing physical assumptions (classical statistics, two-body forces, periodic BC) are domain-specific to a particle-fluid simulation.
Empirical proposition (agreement of MC with virial expansion and free-volume theory; no phase transition observed) is a paper-B physics conclusion with no analogue in paper A.
Logarithmic annealing schedule $T(k)=C/\log(1+k)$ (EP384.2) is paper-A-specific (used in the simulated-annealing experiments). Paper B uses no schedule.
